---
title: "DFS Entry/Exit Times: Subtrees Become Intervals"
description: "Memorisable mathematical reasoning for algorithm interviews, with a worked example and proof."
---

## When to recognise this technique

When questions ask whether one vertex is an ancestor, or need many subtree queries.

## Start with the question

**How can a tree subtree become a contiguous numerical interval?**

## Formula worth memorising

$$
\operatorname{subtree}(v)=[tin(v),tout(v))
$$

**Every symbol explained:** v is a rooted-tree vertex; tin(v) is its index when first visited in DFS preorder; tout(v) is the exclusive end index after processing all descendants. The square/round brackets represent a half-open interval.

**Substitute actual values:** For tree 1→{2,3} with 2→{4}, one preorder is [1,2,4,3]. Then subtree(2) occupies preorder positions [1,3), containing vertices 2 and 4; subtree(3) is [3,4).

## Why the mathematics works

A recursive DFS finishes every child of a vertex before returning, so no unrelated subtree can be interleaved inside that vertex's preorder block. Its block is therefore contiguous, enabling subtree sums by prefix sums over DFS order.

## Limits and counterexamples

This formula uses preorder indices with exclusive subtree ends, not arbitrary wall-clock DFS exit timestamps. For an undirected graph with cycles, a DFS tree is a spanning tree, not the entire graph's ancestor structure.

## The 20-second memory card

**Memorise: DFS makes each rooted-tree subtree a contiguous slice; compute tin and subtree size or exclusive tout, then answer range queries.**

Try explaining the formula aloud using the numerical example, then reproduce the proof from memory. An interview answer must justify the relationship, not just quote it.

**Practice problems:** Subtree Sum Queries; LCA.
